fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From Salmon Clocks to the Teacher Panel", "body": "Bernie Taylor came to cave art as a naturalist asking how salmon and geese keep time without following one smart leader, then looked for that timing in Upper Paleolithic art about 40,000 years old. In a cave in Spain he spotted an elephant and a maned lion he reads as African, and with a friend he met while living in China he says they identified forty or fifty previously unrecognized animals. On one panel he saw an older man speaking into the ear of an apprentice, and asking what story was being told led him to Joseph Campbell and Carl Jung's common dream elements of mountains, rivers and bears."}, {"title": "Why Bernie Thinks Pareidolia Made Us Human", "body": "Bernie Taylor's hypothesis is that what separates us from chimpanzees, Neanderthals and Homo naledi is pareidolia, the capacity to find a pattern and project the psyche into it. There is no bear in the night sky, he says, only a pattern we named and wrapped a Mother Bear story around, and the same instinct finds faces in mountains. Before there were myths, he argues, there was pareidolia, and uniting around shared patterns became a foundation of religion. When Chance Garton notes the skill needs no substance, Bernie agrees: mushrooms give everyone a different vision, while pareidolia gives a group one common image."}, {"title": "A Hero Raised by Mother Animals", "body": "In the panels Bernie Taylor reads, the hero leaves his mother and travels among animals that are mostly mothers guarding their young, a giraffe, a bear, an elephant, and by joining with the young he is protected and taught by them. He slays a lion whose pelt, Bernie says, becomes part of the Hercules myth and whose form becomes Leo. Orion, Perseus and Hercules, Bernie argues, are one character at different stages, with Hercules at the journey's end holding the female animals within his form, anima and animus together. Chance Garton adds that pantheons from Greek to Chinese resolve into mother, father and child, and then into one being."}, {"title": "Bernie's Route From Cave Walls to Ptolemy", "body": "Bernie Taylor lays out three sources for the Greek constellations: their own oral history, around a dozen from the Mesopotamian Mul.Apin, and the bulk from Egypt, carried back by Eudoxus, who studied among the Egyptian priests at the same time as Plato. Bernie says the Paleolithic inventory often paired two asterisms heading north and south, such as a dolphin and a whale the Greeks split into Delphinus and Cetus, and that the International Astronomical Union later separated stars that sat in two constellations at once. Chance Garton recommends a planisphere and H.A. Rey's The Stars; Bernie adds Stellarium."}, {"title": "Where Bernie Locates the First Star Maps", "body": "Bernie Taylor argues that astronomy began on terra firma: people found animals in the rock faces of particular mountains and then placed them in the night sky, which he says is why most constellations make little sense as pictures. He identifies the mountain the Greeks called Atlas as Jebel Toubkal, whose people, today's Amazigh, the ancients called Atlantes, citing Herodotus and a Phoenician account of astronomy being discovered there. Chance Garton adds a linguistic tie between rock and father. Bernie also says a recently publicized South African engraving is exactly the same as one in Iberia, which to him means a culture linked about 36,000 years ago without boats."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Bernie Taylor spent years identifying previously unrecognized animals in 40,000-year-old cave paintings, and found a complete hero's journey encoded in Paleolithic art that became the blueprint for every human mythology that followed. His book Before Orion is the forensic case for this.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Covers paradolia as the evolutionary origin of religion and all human mythology, the Paleolithic cave art hero's journey as the original template for Hercules, Orion, and Perseus, how constellations originated as pareidolia found in mountain rock faces before being mapped to the night sky, the Atlas Mountain as the real Jebel Toubkal and origin of the Atlantis myth, and 36,000-year-old cave art connecting Iberian Spain to South Africa proving prehistoric global connectivity.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From Bonkers to Cited Without Permission", "body": "Bernie Taylor traces four years of academic reception, beginning with total rejection when conference organizers offered him only a poster slot, the place reserved for undergraduates. He advertised those posters on social media, became the last speaker in sessions, then the first, and now gets invited by moderators willing to co-author so his prerecorded talks can play in Europe. He has done more than twenty conferences and posts the only videos of them, so his talks outrank the organizations themselves in search. The final turn came when a Cambridge journal printed work he says lifted his 2004 biological time research without citation."}, {"title": "Reading the Calendar Written Into Cave Animals", "body": "The exclusive hour digs into the biological time work Bernie Taylor published in 2004, before mythology interested him at all. He studied salmon in the Pacific Northwest and found they migrate on dark nights and halt around the full moon, following light and dark cues rather than one smart leader. Applying that to Lascaux, he counted the marks and dots beside each animal as lunations from the vernal equinox, matched them to birthing ibex in May, foaling horses in April, and aurochs dropping calves in July and August. At El Castillo a fledgling golden eagle that has not flown yet dates that panel to mid June."}, {"title": "Everything Keeps Pointing Back to West North Africa", "body": "One mountain anchors the whole hypothesis. The Phoenicians said a man went to Mount Atlas and invented astronomy, and Bernie Taylor identifies that peak as Jebel Toubkal, a glaciated four thousand meter mountain whose rock faces hold most of the constellations in pareidolia. The same region gives us Tifinagh, a written language the Berber or Amazigh people can still read and that matches rock art older than Phoenician or Chinese script. He had a conference talk translated into it and jokes almost nobody watched. Then he points out that a consumer DNA test traces his own earliest ancestry back to those same Amazigh and Tuareg populations."}, {"title": "The Cave as Classroom, Test Chamber and Womb", "body": "Bernie Taylor describes the deep painted galleries as examination rooms rather than galleries. People carried animal marrow fat burning in a shell or wooden bowl, which is why no soot damaged the art, and a teacher stood an apprentice before the panel and asked what the eye sees. The apprentice had to read the animals, the constellations he had known since he was three, and the myths attached to them, because when the teacher died that knowledge had to survive. Chance Garton adds the initiatory reading, that entering the earth replicates the womb and a rebirth, and proposes that caves were the original church."}, {"title": "Science Is Just Mythology With the Trappings Scrubbed Off", "body": "The conversation turns the Big Bang back into a creation myth. Bernie Taylor points out that Father Lemaitre, a Belgian priest and mathematician, built the theory from cosmic egg mythology, that Einstein told him his math was great and his physics atrocious, and that a pope later claimed the singularity proved a creation point. The multiverse, he argues, came from atheist physicists who wanted a different story and can never prove it from inside this one. Chance Garton draws the conclusion that the scientific establishment functions as a priesthood whose cosmogony is no different than the mythos it replaced."}]
